title: Veridian AI — token burst profiling & infra fit
summary: Discovery focused on p95 latency and token-per-second burst behavior for Veridian's real-time summarization product. Customer is evaluating Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private; main concerns are p95 <= 120ms for short-turn prompts, sustained bursts of 1.5k-3k tokens/sec during peak, and streaming jitter for partial outputs. Actionable next steps: Redwood to run a small benchmark plan, share micro-benchmark scripts, and propose a Dedicated pilot with burst capacity. Security docs to be shared for Private option.
next_steps: Redwood to run initial token-burst microbenchmarks on a pinned model and share results (Marcus) — target by 2025-10-16
Sofia to send pricing sketch for Dedicated burst tiers and Hosted SLA notes — by 2025-10-13
Veridian to provide representative prompt set and traffic pattern (Rajesh) — by 2025-10-14
Schedule 45-min technical deep dive with Veridian infra team (Marcus + Maya) — propose slots 2025-10-20/21
action_items: Marcus Li: create and run load script for token burst (openssl-like test harness) against Redwood Hosted and Dedicated staging — due 2025-10-16
Sofia Patel: attach Hosted SLA doc, Dedicated pricing sheet, and Redwood security overview to CRM — due 2025-10-13
Rajesh Kumar: share sample prompts, average seq lengths, and p95 SLO target doc — due 2025-10-14
Maya Torres: grant temporary access to Veridian non-prod VPC for private deployment validation or share traffic replay — due 2025-10-17
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-10-09 15:30 PDT
Duration: 52 mins
Attendees: Sofia (Redwood AE), Marcus (Redwood SE), Hannah (Redwood CSM), Rajesh (Veridian Head of ML), Maya (Platform Eng), Evan (CTO)

Summary section (auto): quick notes about latency/throughput targets, streaming behavior, and next steps.

[00:00] Sofia: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. Quick intros?
[00:10] Rajesh: Hi, Rajesh - head of ML at Veridian. We're building a real-time summarization layer for news and comms and need low latency for short prompts and then burst capacity when trains of articles hit.
[00:22] Maya: Maya from platform, I'll be focused on infra and networking, VPCs, and how we'd run things in-prod.
[00:30] Evan: Evan, CTO, curious about tradeoffs and cost predictability.
[00:35] Sofia: Great. Marcus is our systems SE — he'll walk through how we think about p95s and token/sec behavior. Marcus?
[00:42] Marcus: Thanks. So quick framing: we usually separate two workloads — short interactive queries (10-60 tokens) where p95 matters, and ingestion bursts where you might stream hundreds to thousands of tokens per second. For Hosted we give typical p95 bands, Dedicated adds reserved capacity and better burst isolation, Private is about control/security but depends on your infra.
[01:05] Rajesh: For us specifically, target p95 for short queries is around 100-120ms end-to-end (from client send to first token). For longer summaries we need steady-state throughput — on peak, we anticipate spikes that could look like 1.5k to 3k tokens/sec aggregated across workers.
[01:25] Sofia: Helpful. Are those tokens/sec numbers per user or aggregate across the cluster?
[01:30] Rajesh: Aggregate, across maybe 10-12 workers doing streaming. We also have latency SLO for tail — if p99 crosses 500ms we start to drop quality of experience.
[01:42] Marcus: Okay. A couple of immediate clarifying questions: what's your typical sequence length distribution? How many concurrent user sessions? And are you using streaming partial outputs to the client?
[01:52] Rajesh: Median seq is 40 tokens, 90th is about 320, but our summaries can be 800-1200 tokens on long docs. Concurrency is variable — 200-400 concurrent sessions in normal peaks, but bursts can create a higher transient concurrency. And yes, we stream partial outputs; jitter in chunk arrival is a dealbreaker.
[02:10] Maya: On networking, we need to know TLS handshake costs, and if Redwood supports keep-alive, connection pooling, and whether KV cache warmups are visible to us.
[02:20] Marcus: We do support keep-alive and HTTP/2 streaming; TLS overhead is small compared to token generation for longer sequences, but for short queries it's significant. We have connection pooling recommendations in the SDK. KV cache warming is usually invisible but we provide metrics for cache hits and cold starts.
[02:40] Evan: What's the typical token/sec per GPU you see on public models when serving with our runtime? Rough ballpark.
[02:47] Marcus: Depends on the model and quantization. For a 7B-ish model with our optimized kernels and int8 quant, single GPU steady-state might do 150-300 tokens/sec for autoregressive generation under typical decode configs. For larger models or lower precision the numbers change. But note: we optimize for latency and continuous batching — so real-world client patterns can affect throughput significantly.
[03:12] Rajesh: Hmm, that seems low compared to our internal numbers — we were seeing 400-600 tokens/sec per instance during some tests using a different runtime. Is that because of different batching strategies?
[03:22] Marcus: Could be. Also model architecture, sequence length, and beam/temperature settings matter. There are tradeoffs: pushing more batching increases throughput but hurts p95 for short prompts. We can trade off with Dedicated reserved heap and burst pools to maintain p95 while ramping throughput.
[03:38] Sofia: Can you walk us through an example configuration where p95 stays under 120ms for 40-token queries while allowing bursts to 2k tokens/sec?
[03:47] Marcus: Sure. We usually allocate a small fronting fast-path cluster sized for low-latency interactive requests — optimized for short sequences with minimal batching and aggressive pre-warming. Then a separate pool handles long-running streaming jobs where we allow larger batching. Smart routing sends requests to the right pool based on headers or routing rules. For Dedicated, you can reserve both pools and set autoscale thresholds and burst capacity.
[04:15] Maya: If we do Hosted, what's the isolation like? Could noisy neighbors cause p95 spikes?
[04:22] Marcus: Hosted has multitenant GPU pools but with quota and soft isolation; high variance workloads can cause tail latency. That's exactly where Dedicated or Private shines — Dedicated reserve capacity avoids noisy neighbor effects; Private gives you full control. We also support fallback policies: if Dedicated micro-pool is saturated, you can route to a compatible lower-cost model to prevent failures.
[04:45] Rajesh: You'll need to show us real numbers — ideally with our prompts. Will Redwood run tests?
[04:50] Sofia: Yes, we can run microbenchmarks. Marcus will draft a small script to replay your prompts across concurrency patterns. Two variants: a short-query p95 test and a burst-stream test that measures sustained tokens/sec and streaming jitter.
[05:05] Marcus: Proposed plan: you give us a sample prompt set and a traffic shape file (we can accept JSON or a CSV with timestamps). We'll run against Hosted staging and a Dedicated-like isolated cluster in our lab; measure p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, connection RTT, and streaming inter-chunk latency distribution. We'll also capture cold-start behavior.
[05:30] Maya: If we provide a VPC peering or a short-lived bastion for private testing, could you run the same tests against an on-prem deployment?
[05:38] Marcus: Yes — for Private we'll need either a staging VPC connection or an offline artifact we can run in your environment. There are more variables (networking, GPU type) but it's doable.
[05:48] Evan: Cost-wise, what's the delta between Hosted burst usage and Dedicated reserved capacity?
[05:54] Sofia: Very high-level: Hosted is pay-as-you-go and can be cheaper for low average utilization but expensive in sustained burst scenarios. Dedicated has a monthly commit but yields much lower per-token cost and predictable tail behavior. We'll share a sketch with example math for your traffic profile.
[06:12] Rajesh: Two other things: 1) encryption at rest and key management — do you support KMS/HSM for Private? 2) audit logs and per-token attribution for compliance.
[06:23] Marcus: Private supports customer-managed KMS/HSM integrations and full audit logs with token-level metadata if required. For Hosted we offer encrypted storage and can integrate with enterprise KMS via connectors for Dedicated and Private. We'll attach our security pack.
[06:38] Rajesh: Good. On model selection: we plan to start with an open LLM (we have a fine-tuned base) but may evaluate larger proprietary models. How easy is model swap and fallback?
[06:47] Marcus: Our runtime supports multiple models and automatic fallback to smaller compatible variants. You can pin versions; rollouts are supported with canary traffic. For Dedicated we can stage both models and route based on SLOs.
[06:58] Maya: About streaming jitter — do you measure inter-chunk timing? Our clients consider any >200ms inter-chunk gap as perceived stall.
[07:07] Marcus: We measure inter-chunk latency and provide histograms. In the benchmark we'll surface 50/95/99 of inter-chunk gaps. We'll also measure first-byte times.
[07:20] Rajesh: For the burst test, we need to ensure the runtime can sustain 3k tokens/sec for at least two minutes without p95 degradation — that's our worst-case run. Can you simulate bursts like that?
[07:30] Marcus: Yes, we'll set sustained traffic shapes. If Dedicated hasn't got enough reserved capacity, we might recommend a small burst pool or pre-warmed pods. We'll record the token/sec before and after background load and show the effect.
[07:45] Evan: Any limitations with HTTP/2 streaming that we should know?
[07:50] Marcus: Mostly client-side; we support gRPC and HTTP/2 streams. We suggest connection pooling, reuse, and small chunk sizes for steady streaming. Also watch for platform-level load balancers that terminate HTTP/2 unexpectedly.
[08:05] Rajesh: Let's talk about observability. We need token-level cost breakdown, latency per route, and per-request traces.
[08:14] Hannah: On Redwood Console you'll get per-route token and latency breakdowns, traces, and an events stream. We can set retention policies. For the pilot we'll enable developer-level dashboards and share access.
[08:30] Maya: How about KV cache behavior — does it persist across restarts, and how do you surface cache hit ratio?
[08:36] Marcus: KV cache in our runtime is RAM-backed; for Dedicated we can enable warm+persist policies and surface hit ratios in metrics. Cold starts show in traces.
[08:48] Rajesh: Any recommended decode configs to reduce token/sec cost without impacting quality?
[08:56] Marcus: Beam search vs sampling tradeoffs — often lowering temperature and tweaking max tokens and top-k can reduce generation load. Quantization and pruning also help. We'll include model-specific guidance after we see the sample prompts.
[09:10] Sofia: Quick pause — Is everyone aligned on deliverables? We will need the prompt set and traffic shape; Marcus will run the tests and share a short report; Sofia will send pricing/security; Veridian will review and we reconvene.
[09:22] Rajesh: Yes. Can you also include an option for burst autoscaling with a 1-2 minute cold-start safe window? We need to understand the safety and how cold starts affect p95.
[09:33] Marcus: Absolutely — we'll include cold-start timing curves and suggestions like pre-warm predicates, and ephemeral burst pools.
[09:42] Evan: On SLA — do you have p95 commitments for Hosted or are they more guidance?
[09:47] Sofia: Hosted has published latency bands but Dedicated offers an SLA for throughput/availability; we'll attach the detailed SLA doc.
[09:55] Maya: For Private, what's the support model for upgrades/patches?
[10:00] Hannah: Private includes an enterprise support plan; upgrades can be coordinated windows. We provide runbooks and optional managed upgrade service.
[10:08] Rajesh: Ok we want a sample benchmark run inside two weeks and a pricing sketch in a few days.
[10:14] Sofia: We'll do that. Any other concerns?
[10:18] Maya: Network egress cost — if we stream a lot of tokens out, who ends up paying? We need to model egress costs for Hosted vs Private.
[10:26] Sofia: We'll add egress estimates to the pricing sketch.
[10:30] Marcus: A couple of gotchas to call out — token accounting differences across models and tokenizers; we'll normalize token counts in our report and show raw vs normalized TPS. Also watch for tail amplification if you use long contexts.
[10:45] Rajesh: Good note. For data retention, can we set retention windows per environment?
[10:49] Hannah: Yes, for Dedicated and Private you can configure retention policies; Hosted has default retention with add-on retention.
[10:58] Evan: Ok, let's lock on dates. Sofia — send proposed deep-dive slots for Oct 20/21.
[11:05] Sofia: Will do. Marcus any notes on the microbench harness we should mention?
[11:09] Marcus: The harness will replay prompts with exact inter-arrival times, track first-byte and inter-chunk latencies, count tokens produced, and measure per-request CPU/GPU utilization when we have infra access. We'll publish a short README and the script.
[11:24] Rajesh: Great. One last thing — can you show a worst-case scenario where a background retrain or heavy batch job causes p95 spikes and how Redwood mitigates it?
[11:33] Marcus: We'll include a simulated background load and show routing/fallback behaviors and how Dedicated burst pools absorb the load.
[11:44] Sofia: Thanks all. We'll follow up with a pack: benchmark plan, security docs, pricing, and proposed pilot scope.
[11:50] Evan: Thanks everyone.
[11:52] End of call.

Notes about transcript quality: occasional mis-transcriptions around model names and acronyms; speaker overlaps minimal.
